mainTopic: The end of פרק שבועת הפקדון, and the opening of שבועת הדיינין: when one who admits part of a claim must swear, and how the court administers the oath
overview: The גמרא finishes asking whether a man who swore to one claimant and then said 'and not yours either' to the others is liable for each claim separately. From רבי חייא's count of twenty offerings it concludes that such a denial counts as specific. It then explains why רבי שמעון exempts a false oath about rape or seduction. אביי knocks down רבא's grain parable, and רבין's version of רבי יוחנן says that according to רבי שמעון the father claims only the קנס. That ends פרק שבועת הפקדון. A new משנה opens the laws of שבועת הדיינין, the oath of one who admits part of a claim: the minimum amounts, full denial versus partial admission, and when the admission counts as the same kind as the claim. It also covers vessels and land, and whose claims can lead to an oath. The גמרא then teaches that the person swearing must hold a holy object, and the הלכה follows רבא and not רב פפא. It adds rules for standing or sitting, and says the oath may be said in any language. The judges' warning before the oath begins here and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Or is he liable for each claim separately?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its question by giving the second possibility: maybe he is liable for every single claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or perhaps he is liable for each and every one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a question that started before this section. It offers the second side: maybe the defendant is liable separately for each claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case: he swore clearly to the first claimant, then told the others 'and not yours either.' One side says this is one general oath, so there is one liability. This line gives the other side: each 'and not yours' counts as its own specific oath, so there is a separate liability for each.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps (introduces the second side of a question)

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא אַכׇּל חֲדָא וַחֲדָא מִיחַיַּיב?
phrases.english: Or perhaps he is liable for each and every one?

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹ דִלְמָא אַכׇּל חֲדָא וַחֲדָא מִיחַיַּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a question that began before this section
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'and not yours either' to each extra claimant count as a separate specific oath, making him liable for each claim?

steps.title: רבי חייא's teaching: twenty sin-offerings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא of רבי חייא that says the defendant brings twenty חטאות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear what רבי חייא taught: Here there are twenty sin-offerings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to answer the question: רבי חייא counts twenty sin-offerings in this kind of case. It is setting up the proof, which it works out in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A high count means he is liable many separate times, not just once. The next step asks what case רבי חייא must be talking about.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rabbi Chiyya taught:
Here there are twenty sin-offerings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to answer the question in step 1
steps.raayaObject: That each claim brings a separate liability
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי חייא counting twenty sin-offerings

steps.title: Working out the case: he did not specify, yet he is liable many times
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that רבי חייא cannot mean a case where each oath was fully spelled out, so he must mean the 'and not yours' case. That case therefore counts as specific.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If he spelled out each oath, did רבי חייא come only to teach us a number? Rather, it must be where he did not spell it out. Learn from this that it counts as specific.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what case the ברייתא is about. It rules out the obvious case and concludes that 'and not yours either' counts as a specific oath for each claimant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he swore clearly to each claim, twenty liabilities is obvious, and רבי חייא would just be doing math. So the ברייתא must be teaching something new: even when he swore clearly only to the first and said 'and not yours' to the rest, each one counts on its own. That answers the question with the second option from step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How do we picture it?

steps.whatToRemember: Saying 'and not yours either' to each extra claimant counts as a specific oath, so he is liable for each claim separately.

phrases.english: What is the case?
If he spelled it out,
phrases.notes: He means he swore a full, clear oath to each claimant about each claim.

phrases.english: did Rabbi Chiyya come to teach us a number?
Rather, is it not where he did not spell it out?
phrases.notes: He swore clearly only to the first, then said 'and not yours' to the others.

phrases.english: And learn from this that it counts as specific.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Works out the case of the ברייתא from step 2 to complete the proof
steps.raayaObject: That 'and not yours either' counts as a specific oath
steps.raayaSupportSource: A count of twenty would teach nothing new unless the case is one where he did not spell out each oath
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Such a denial counts as פרטא, so he is liable for each claim.

steps.title: Why רבי שמעון exempts in the case of rape or seduction
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the משנה about 'you raped or seduced my daughter.' רבי יוחנן explains that רבי שמעון exempts because the father's main claim is the קנס.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You raped or seduced my daughter,' etc. רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: What is רבי שמעון's reason? Since the main thing he is claiming is the fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting the משנה. It gives רבי יוחנן's explanation of why רבי שמעון says a false oath here does not make the defendant liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father could claim the קנס and also payments like shame and damage, which are ordinary money. The חכמים make him liable because of those money payments. רבי שמעון looks at what the father is mainly after, which is the קנס. Since the oath is really about the fine, the defendant is exempt.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי שמעון does not say the father has no money claim at all. He says the main claim is the קנס, and that is what decides the case.

phrases.english: "You raped or seduced my daughter," etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. The 'etc.' points to the rest of it, where רבי שמעון exempts and the חכמים make him liable.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
What is the reason of Rabbi Shimon?
Since it is mainly the fine that he is claiming.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שמעון exempts because the father's main claim is the קנס, and the other payments are secondary.

steps.title: רבא's parable: wheat, barley and spelt
steps.stepSummary: רבא compares רבי שמעון's reasoning to a man who claims three kinds of grain, and the other swears only about the wheat. The wheat oath was true, so he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: What is רבי שמעון's view like? Like a man who said to his friend, 'Give me the wheat, barley and spelt of mine that you have.' The friend said, 'I swear you have no wheat with me.' It turned out he really had no wheat, but he did have the barley and spelt. He is exempt, because when he swore about the wheat, he swore the truth.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a parable to make רבי שמעון's reasoning easy to picture.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claim had three parts, but the oath covered only one, the wheat, and that oath was true. So even though he did hold the barley and spelt, he never swore falsely about them and is exempt. In the same way, the defendant's oath is judged by what it was really about, which according to רבי שמעון is the קנס.

keyTerms.meaning: It was found, it turned out

steps.whatToRemember: An oath is judged by what it actually covered. If what he swore about was true, he is exempt even if other parts of the claim were valid.

phrases.english: Rava said: The parable for Rabbi Shimon's view,
what is the matter like?
To a person who said to his fellow:
"Give me the wheat, barley and spelt
of mine that are in your hand,"

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: ״שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁאֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי חִטִּין״;
phrases.english: he said to him: "I swear you have no wheat in my hand";
and it turned out that it was wheat that he did not have,
but barley and spelt he did have,
that he is exempt;
because when he swore about the wheat, he swore about the truth.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָשָׁל דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates רבי יוחנן's explanation of רבי שמעון with a parable
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the oath covered only a part of the claim and that part was true, he is exempt, even if other parts of the claim were valid.

steps.title: אביי rejects רבא's grain comparison
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues that the grain case is not like our case. In our case the defendant denied everything, so his oath was false about the בושת and פגם too.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: Are these cases really alike? In the grain case, he denied only the wheat and did not deny the barley and spelt. Here he denied the whole thing! Our case is really like someone who says, 'Give me my wheat, barley and spelt,' and the other swears, 'You have nothing of yours with me at all.' Then it turns out only the wheat was not there, but the barley and spelt were. In that case he is liable!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבא's comparison from Step 5. He says the grain case does not match the case of the daughter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבא's grain case, the oath was only about the wheat, and that part was true. In our case the man swore 'I never raped or seduced her.' That denies the בושת and פגם payments too, and he really does owe those. So the right comparison is someone who swore 'I have nothing of yours,' which was false about the barley and spelt. He would be liable, and that cannot explain why רבי שמעון exempts.

keyTerms.meaning: Are they comparable? A standard way to reject a comparison.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse the two grain cases. In רבא's case the oath covered only the wheat, which was true. In אביי's case the oath covered everything ('nothing at all'), so it was false about the barley and spelt.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: Are they comparable?!
phrases.notes: 'Him' is רבא, whose grain comparison was in Step 5.

phrases.english: There, he denies him regarding the wheat,

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׂעוֹרִין וְכוּסְּמִין לָא קָא כָפַר לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: but regarding barley and spelt he does not deny him.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא – בְּכוּלַּהּ מִילְּתָא הוּא דְּקָא כָפַר לֵיהּ!
phrases.english: Here, it is the entire matter that he denies him!

phrases.aramaic: הָא לָא דָּמְיָא אֶלָּא לְאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ:
phrases.english: This is comparable only to one who says to his fellow:
"Give me wheat and barley and spelt
that I have in your possession,"
and he answered: "An oath that you have nothing in my possession at all";
and it turned out that it is only wheat that he does not have,

phrases.aramaic: הָא שְׂעוֹרִין וְכוּסְּמִין אִית לֵיהּ – דְּמִיחַיַּיב!
phrases.english: but barley and spelt he does have, and there he is liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's comparison from Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's comparison of רבי שמעון's case to the true oath about wheat alone.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The defendant's denial covered everything, including the בושת and פגם he really owes. So his oath was partly false about real money, and he should be liable.

steps.title: רבין's version: רבי שמעון says the father claims only the fine
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports רבי יוחנן differently. According to רבי שמעון the father claims only the קנס, while the חכמים say he also claims בושת and פגם.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רבין came, he said that רבי יוחנן said: According to רבן שמעון, the father claims only the fine, not humiliation and degradation. According to the חכמים, he also claims humiliation and degradation.
steps.whatsHappening: After אביי's attack, the גמרא drops the earlier explanation. It brings a new version of רבי יוחנן's words from רבין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the dispute is about what the father is actually claiming. If he claims only the קנס, the oath covers only the קנס, and that is not a regular money claim. So רבי שמעון exempts. The חכמים say the claim also includes בושת and פגם, which are real money, so the oath does make him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: When רבין came from ארץ ישראל to בבל and reported a teaching
A fixed fine set by the Torah
Payment for the loss in value (degradation)

steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes the accepted explanation of the dispute in the משנה. It moves the argument from 'how much did he deny' to 'what was the father claiming in the first place.'

phrases.english: Rather, when Ravin came,
he said that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: לְדִבְרֵי רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן – קְנָס הוּא תּוֹבֵעַ,
phrases.english: According to Rabban Shimon, it is the fine that he claims,
phrases.notes: The text says רבן שמעון here, but it means the same רבי שמעון from the משנה.

phrases.english: and not humiliation and degradation;
according to the Sages,
he also claims humiliation and degradation.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the explanation that אביי knocked down with a new version of רבי יוחנן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שמעון: the father claims only the קנס. חכמים: he also claims בושת and פגם.

steps.title: What is the reason behind their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what principle splits רבי שמעון and the חכמים about what the father claims.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It asks for the reasoning behind each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 told us what each side holds, but not why. Here the גמרא asks what idea leads each side to read the father's claim differently.

keyTerms.meaning: About what do they disagree? It asks for the root of a dispute.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רבין's report.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The principle behind the dispute over what the father is claiming.

steps.title: רב פפא: fixed amount versus what admission cancels
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains each side. רבי שמעון says a person prefers to claim a fixed amount. The חכמים say a person would not give up a claim that admission cannot cancel.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: רבי שמעון holds that a person does not give up something with a fixed amount and claim something without a fixed amount. And the רבנן hold that a person does not give up something he still gets even if the other admits, and claim only something that the other is exempt from if he admits.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question from Step 8 by giving the logic of each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קנס is a fixed fifty שקלים, while בושת and פגם have to be assessed. So רבי שמעון says the father would claim only the sure, fixed קנס. The חכמים point out that if the defendant admits, he is exempt from the קנס but still owes בושת and פגם. So the father would surely claim those too.

keyTerms.meaning: A person does not give up (a claim)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון: a person goes for the fixed amount (קנס). חכמים: a person goes for what admission cannot cancel (בושת and פגם), so he claims both.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two ideas. 'Fixed' points to the קנס. 'Not cancelled by admitting' points to בושת and פגם, because admitting to a קנס exempts you from paying it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן סָבַר:
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: Rabbi Shimon holds:
A person does not leave aside something that is fixed
phrases.notes: The קנס is a set amount, while בושת and פגם have to be assessed.

phrases.english: and claim something that is not fixed.
And the Rabbis hold:

phrases.aramaic: לָא שָׁבֵיק מִידֵּי דְּכִי מוֹדֵה בֵּיהּ לָא מִיפְּטַר,
phrases.english: He does not leave aside something from which the other is not exempt if he admits it,

phrases.aramaic: וְתָבַע מִידֵּי דְּכִי מוֹדֵה בֵּיהּ מִיפְּטַר.
phrases.english: and claim something from which he is exempt if he admits it.
phrases.notes: Someone who admits on his own to owing a קנס is exempt from paying it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן סָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי שמעון: people claim the fixed amount (קנס). חכמים: people would not give up the claim that admission cannot cancel (בושת and פגם).

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter on the oath of deposits
steps.stepSummary: The closing line of פרק שבועת הפקדון.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'The Oath of Deposits.'
steps.whatsHappening: This line closes the פרק of שבועת הפקדון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion of false oaths denying money ends here. The next line opens a new פרק about a different kind of oath.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you, the line said when finishing a פרק
A false oath denying money one holds, and the name of this פרק

phrases.english: We will return to you, chapter 'The Oath of Deposits'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the פרק.

steps.title: New משנה: the minimum amounts for the court's oath
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה sets the rules for שבועת הדיינין. The claim must be at least two silver מעה, the admission at least a פרוטה, and the admission must be the same kind as the claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: The oath of the judges applies when the claim is for two silver coins and the admission is worth a פרוטה. And if the admission is not the same type as the claim, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק opens. The משנה lists the basic conditions for the oath that the court gives to someone who admits part of a claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three conditions are given. The claim must be at least two silver מעה. The part he admits must be worth at least a פרוטה. And what he admits must be the same kind of thing that was claimed. Without these, there is no oath.

keyTerms.meaning: The oath imposed by the court, here on someone who admits part of a claim
Worth a פרוטה, the smallest coin

steps.whyThisMatters: These are the basic conditions for the oath of מודה במקצת, and the coming גמרא builds on them.

phrases.english: Mishnah: The oath of the judges:
the claim is two silver,
phrases.notes: 'Two silver' means two silver מעה coins. The word מעה is left out.

phrases.english: and the admission is worth a peruta.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אֵין הַהוֹדָאָה מִמִּין הַטַּעֲנָה – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: And if the admission is not of the type of the claim, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new פרק after the הדרן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court's oath requires a claim of at least two silver מעה, an admission worth at least a פרוטה, and an admission of the same type as the claim.

steps.title: Examples of the minimum claim and admission amounts
steps.stepSummary: The משנה illustrates the two-silver and פרוטה rule. A claim of exactly שתי כסף with an admission of a פרוטה is exempt. A claim of שתי כסף and a פרוטה with an admission of a פרוטה is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? If he says 'I have two silver מעה with you' and the other says 'You only have a פרוטה with me,' he is exempt. If he says 'I have two silver מעה and a פרוטה with you' and the other says 'You only have a פרוטה with me,' he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks 'how so?' and gives two side-by-side cases to show how the rule of step 11 works in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases differ by only one פרוטה in the claim, and that one פרוטה changes the result from exempt to liable. The משנה gives no reason here. The גמרא later discusses exactly why the first case is exempt, so for now just learn the two outcomes side by side.

keyTerms.meaning: Two silver מעה, the minimum claim
The smallest coin, the minimum admission

steps.confusionAlert: Both cases have the same admission (a פרוטה). The only thing that changes is the size of the claim, and that one extra פרוטה flips the result from exempt to liable.

phrases.english: How so?
'I have two silver coins in your possession,'
phrases.notes: 'Two silver' means two silver מעה, the minimum claim from step 11.

phrases.english: 'You have only a פרוטה in my possession' –
he is exempt.
'I have two silver coins and a פרוטה in your possession,'
'You have only a פרוטה in my possession' –
he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives concrete examples of the amount rules stated in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A claim of two silver with a פרוטה admitted is exempt; a claim of two silver plus a פרוטה with a פרוטה admitted is liable.

steps.title: Full denial versus partial admission
steps.stepSummary: If the defendant denies the whole מנה, he is exempt from the oath. If he admits fifty דינר of it, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I have a מנה with you.' 'You have nothing with me' – exempt. 'I have a מנה with you.' 'You only have fifty דינר with me' – liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה contrasts a defendant who denies everything with one who admits part of the claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath of the תורה comes only when the defendant admits some of the claim and denies the rest. Denying everything does not trigger it. Admitting half does.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred דינר
One who admits part of a claim

steps.whatToRemember: Full denial = no oath here. Partial admission = oath.

phrases.english: 'I have a מנה in your possession,'
'You have nothing in my possession' –
he is exempt.
'I have a מנה in your possession,'
'You have only fifty דינר in my possession' –
he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the minimum amounts to the basic contrast between full denial and partial admission.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A defendant who denies the whole claim is exempt from this oath; one who admits part is liable.

steps.title: A claim on behalf of a late father
steps.stepSummary: When a son claims a מנה that was owed to his father, and the defendant admits fifty, the defendant is exempt. He is treated like someone returning a lost item.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'My father had a מנה with you.' 'You only have fifty דינר with me' – exempt, because he is like one returning a lost item.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a case that looks like partial admission but is still exempt, and explains why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son does not know the facts himself, so the defendant could easily have denied everything. By admitting fifty on his own, he acts like an honest finder returning a lost object, so we do not make him swear.

keyTerms.meaning: A מנה that belonged to my father
Like one who returns a lost item

steps.confusionAlert: The admission here is the same as in step 13 (fifty out of a מנה). What changes the result is that the claim comes from the son about his father's money.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that partial admission alone does not always bring an oath; a voluntary honest admission is rewarded, not punished.

phrases.english: 'My father had a מנה in your possession,'
'You have only fifty דינר in my possession' –
he is exempt,
because he is like one returning a lost item.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an exception to the partial-admission rule of step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A partial admission to a son's claim about his father's debt does not obligate an oath, since the defendant is like one returning a lost item.

steps.title: Admitting a debt and then claiming payment or denial
steps.stepSummary: After admitting a מנה, if the next day the defendant says 'I gave it to you,' he is exempt. If he says 'You have nothing with me,' he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I have a מנה with you.' He said 'Yes.' The next day the lender said 'Give it to me.' If he answers 'I already gave it to you' – exempt. If he answers 'You have nothing with me' – liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה looks at a defendant who first admits the debt and then, the next day, answers in one of two ways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'I paid you' does not contradict yesterday's admission, so he is believed. Saying 'You have nothing with me' denies that the debt ever existed, which contradicts his own admission, so he must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: I already gave it to you

steps.whatToRemember: After admitting a debt: 'I paid' is believed; 'There never was a debt' is not.

phrases.english: 'I have a מנה in your possession,'
he said to him: 'Yes';
the next day he said to him: 'Give it to me,'
'I gave it to you' –
he is exempt.
'You have nothing in my possession' –
he is liable.
phrases.notes: Liable to pay, since he already admitted the debt yesterday.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָנֶה לִי בְּיָדְךָ אָמַר לוֹ הֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new kind of case: a defendant who already admitted the debt and later answers differently.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A defendant who admitted a debt is believed if he later says he paid, but is liable if he later denies the debt existed.

steps.title: A loan that must be repaid in front of witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The defendant admitted a מנה, and the lender said 'only pay me in front of עדים.' Later the defendant says 'I paid you.' He must pay, because he did not pay in front of עדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The lender said, 'I have a מנה with you,' and the borrower said, 'Yes.' The lender said, 'Only give it back to me in front of witnesses.' The next day the lender said, 'Give it to me,' and the borrower answered, 'I already gave it to you.' The borrower must pay, because he was required to repay it in front of witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives one more case of a defendant who first admits a loan and later says he already paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 15, 'I gave it to you' got the defendant off. Here it does not, because the lender set a condition: repayment had to be done in front of עדים. A payment without עדים does not count, so his claim of paying privately does not help him, and he must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: I already gave it to you (I already repaid)

steps.confusionAlert: Here חייב means he must actually pay the money. In the next steps חייב means he must take a שבועה. Read each case by its context.

phrases.english: "I have a maneh in your hand," and he said to him "Yes";
"Do not give it to me except in front of witnesses,"
the next day he said to him "Give it to me,"
"I gave it to you": he is liable,
phrases.notes: Liable here means he has to pay the מנה, not just swear.

phrases.english: because he needed to give it in front of witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: An exception to step 15: there, 'I gave it to you' exempts him; here a condition to repay in front of עדים makes him liable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the lender required repayment in front of עדים, a claim of repaying without עדים does not help, and the borrower must pay.

steps.title: Gold and silver: a different kind versus the same kind
steps.stepSummary: Claiming a לטרא of gold and admitting a לטרא of silver is a different kind, so there is no שבועה. Claiming a gold דינר and admitting silver coins counts as the same kind, because all are coins, so he must take a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he claims, 'I have a לטרא of gold with you,' and the defendant says, 'You only have a לטרא of silver with me,' he is exempt. If he claims, 'I have a gold דינר with you,' and the defendant says, 'You only have a silver דינר, a טריסית, a פונדיון, and a פרוטה with me,' he is liable, because they are all one kind: coins.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה uses two cases to show the rule from step 11 that the admission must be the same kind as the claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A לטרא is a weight of metal, so gold and silver are two separate kinds of material. Once the admission is a different kind, it is not a partial admission. A gold דינר is a coin, and coins are all one kind of thing, money. So admitting smaller silver coins counts as admitting part of the claim, and he must take a שבועה.

keyTerms.meaning: A litra, a fixed weight of metal
A small coin, smaller than a טריסית
The category of coins, all one kind

phrases.english: "I have a litra of gold in your hand,"

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי אֶלָּא לִיטְרָא כֶּסֶף״ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: "You have nothing in my hand except a litra of silver": he is exempt.
"I have a gold dinar in your hand,"
"You have nothing in my hand except a silver dinar
and a tereisit and pundeyons and a peruta": he is liable,
phrases.notes: Liable here means he must take a שבועה.

phrases.english: because they are all one kind: coins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the repayment cases to illustrating the 'same kind' rule set in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Raw gold and raw silver are different kinds, so there is no שבועה. All coins are one kind, so a שבועה is required.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that 'same kind' depends on what the claim is really about. A claim about coins is about money, so any coin counts.

steps.title: Grain versus produce: does the claim include legumes?
steps.stepSummary: Claiming a כור of grain and admitting legumes is a different kind, so he is exempt. Claiming a כור of produce and admitting legumes is liable, because legumes are included in 'produce.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If he claims, 'I have a כור of grain with you,' and the defendant says, 'You only have a לתך of legumes with me,' he is exempt. If he claims, 'I have a כור of produce with you,' and the defendant says, 'You only have a לתך of legumes with me,' he is liable, because legumes are included in produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives another pair of cases. Whether the defendant must swear depends on how the claimant worded his claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word תבואה means grain, and legumes are not grain, so admitting legumes is a different kind. The word פירות is a wide category that includes legumes. So the same admission counts as part of the claim and requires a שבועה.

keyTerms.meaning: Legumes, such as beans and lentils

phrases.english: "I have a kor of grain in your hand,"

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי אֶלָּא לֶתֶךְ קִטְנִית״ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: "You have nothing in my hand except a half-kor of legumes": he is exempt.
"I have a kor of produce in your hand,"

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי אֶלָּא לֶתֶךְ קִטְנִית״ – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: "You have nothing in my hand except a half-kor of legumes": he is liable,
because legumes are included in produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second pair of cases for the 'same kind' rule, this time with food instead of metal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the claim is 'grain,' admitting legumes is a different kind. If the claim is 'produce,' legumes are included, so a שבועה is required.

steps.title: Wheat claimed, barley admitted: רבן גמליאל disagrees
steps.stepSummary: If he claimed wheat and the defendant admitted barley, the anonymous view exempts him. רבן גמליאל says he must take a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he claimed wheat from him, and the defendant admitted to barley, he is exempt. And רבן גמליאל makes him liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה states the basic 'different kind' case and then brings רבן גמליאל, who disagrees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the anonymous view, wheat and barley are different kinds, so admitting barley is not a partial admission. רבן גמליאל requires a שבועה anyway. This shows that, in his view, the admission does not have to be the same kind as the claim.
steps.whatToRemember: The anonymous view requires the admission to be the same kind as the claim (gold and silver, grain and legumes, wheat and barley are all different kinds). רבן גמליאל requires a שבועה even when the admission is a different kind.

phrases.english: If he claimed wheat from him,
and he admitted to him barley: he is exempt.
And Rabban Gamliel holds him liable.
phrases.notes: He means liable to take a שבועה, even though barley is a different kind from wheat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the plainest 'different kind' case and records רבן גמליאל's disagreement with the whole rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The anonymous view exempts someone who admits a different kind than what was claimed. רבן גמליאל requires a שבועה even then.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the 'same kind' requirement from step 11 is disputed, and רבן גמליאל disagrees with it.

steps.title: Jugs of oil versus empty jugs
steps.stepSummary: Someone claims jugs of oil and the defendant admits only the jugs. אדמון says he must swear because the admission is part of the same kind as the claim. The חכמים say it is a different kind. רבן גמליאל agrees with אדמון.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone claims jugs of oil from his friend and the friend admits to owing the jugs, אדמון says: since he admitted part of the same kind as the claim, he must swear. The חכמים say: the admission is not the same kind as the claim. רבן גמליאל said: I agree with אדמון.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings another case about whether an admission counts as 'part of the claim.' Here the claim is for jugs full of oil, and the defendant admits only to the jugs themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אדמון sees the jugs as part of what was claimed, so this is a partial admission and the defendant must swear. The חכמים see the claim as really being about oil, so admitting the containers is a different item and there is no oath. רבן גמליאל sides with אדמון, which fits his view in Step 19, where he also requires an oath even when the admitted item is not exactly what was claimed.

keyTerms.meaning: Jugs of oil. This can mean jugs full of oil, or the jugs that hold oil.
Jugs or earthenware containers, here the empty jugs themselves.
Of the same kind as the claim. An admission must be of this kind to require an oath.
A judge in ירושלים whose rulings appear in the משנה.

phrases.english: One who claims from his fellow jugs of oil,
phrases.notes: He means jugs filled with oil. The question is whether the claim is about the oil or also about the jugs.

phrases.english: and the other admitted to him the jugs,
Admon says:
Since he admitted to him part
of the same kind as the claim, he must swear.
And the Sages say:
The admission is not of the same kind as the claim.
Rabban Gamliel said:
I see the words of Admon as correct.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's series of 'same kind or different kind' cases, now with containers and their contents.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדמון and רבן גמליאל: admitting the jugs counts as part of the claim, so he swears. The חכמים: it is a different kind, so he is exempt.

steps.title: Claims of vessels and land
steps.stepSummary: There is no oath over land. Admitting the vessels and denying the land (or the reverse) is exempt, and admitting part of the land is exempt. Admitting part of the vessels requires an oath, and the movable property pulls the land into the oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he claimed vessels and land, and the defendant admitted the vessels and denied the land, or admitted the land and denied the vessels, he is exempt. If he admitted part of the land, he is exempt. If he admitted part of the vessels, he is liable, because property without a guarantee (movables) binds property with a guarantee (land) to be sworn on as well.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה deals with a claim that mixes movable items (vessels) with land, and explains when an oath is required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Oaths are not taken over land. So when the admission and the denial split cleanly between land and vessels, or when the partial admission is about the land, there is no oath. But if he admits part of the vessels, there is a real partial admission on movables. He must swear on the vessels, and that oath also brings in the land.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarantee. Land is 'property with אחריות' because a lender can collect from it.
Bind or pull in. Here it means the oath on movables extends to the land.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the land is ignored in the last case. When he admits part of the vessels, the oath also covers the land claim.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the משנה's source for an oath on one item pulling in a related claim that would otherwise not need an oath.

phrases.english: If he claimed from him vessels and land,
and he admitted the vessels and denied the land,
or admitted the land and denied the vessels, he is exempt.
If he admitted part of the land, he is exempt.
If he admitted part of the vessels, he is liable,
because property that does not serve as a guarantee
phrases.notes: This means movable things like vessels, which a lender cannot reliably collect from.

phrases.aramaic: זוֹקְקִין אֶת הַנְּכָסִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶן אַחְרָיוּת
phrases.english: binds the property that does serve as a guarantee
to swear about them too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from 'same kind' questions to the type of property: movables versus land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No oath over land alone. A partial admission of the vessels requires an oath, and that oath extends to the land.

steps.title: No oath on claims of a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor
steps.stepSummary: No oath is taken on a claim brought by a חרש, שוטה, or קטן, and a קטן is not made to swear. But one does swear to a קטן and to הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor, and we do not make a minor swear. But we do swear to a minor and to הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה closes by listing whose claims can lead to an oath, and who can be made to swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A claim made by a חרש, שוטה, or קטן does not obligate the defendant to swear, and a קטן is never the one who swears. Still, the משנה says one does swear to a קטן and to הקדש. When there is a valid basis for an oath, the defendant swears even though the other side is a minor or הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: A deaf-mute, treated as lacking full legal understanding.
A person who is mentally incompetent.
Property dedicated to the בית המקדש.

steps.confusionAlert: 'Swearing on the claim of a minor' and 'swearing to a minor' are different. The minor's own claim does not create an oath, but an oath can still be owed to him.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה ends with three rules: no oath on the claim of a חרש, שוטה, or קטן; a קטן never swears; but one swears to a קטן and to הקדש.

phrases.english: One does not take an oath on the claim of
a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor,
and one does not make a minor take an oath;
but one does take an oath to a minor and to the Temple property.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל טַעֲנַת חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the type of property to the type of people involved in the claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No oath on the claim of a חרש, שוטה, or קטן, and no oath imposed on a קטן, but an oath is taken to a קטן and to הקדש.

steps.title: How is the oath administered?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking how the court has the person swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: How do we make him swear?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and asks a practical question: what exact form of oath does the court use? This sets up רב's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the משנה only said who must swear. The גמרא now asks about the procedure: which words and which Name the oath uses.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that analyzes the משנה.

phrases.english: Gemara: How do we make him swear?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the משנה's rules to the procedure of the oath.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact form in which the court administers an oath.

steps.title: רב: the oath stated in the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: the court uses the oath described in the Torah, as in אברהם's words to his servant, 'I will make you swear by ה׳, God of heaven.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: We make him swear with the oath stated in the Torah, as it is written: 'And I will make you swear by ה׳, the God of heaven.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question: the court uses the same kind of oath that appears in the Torah, swearing by God's Name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is the פסוק where אברהם makes his servant swear 'by ה׳, God of heaven.' This shows that a proper oath is made by invoking God's Name, and the court follows that model.

keyTerms.meaning: The oath stated in the Torah.
And I will make you swear.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
We make him swear with the oath
that is stated in the Torah,
as it is written:
"And I will make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven."
phrases.notes: בראשית 24:3

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The court administers the Torah's form of oath, invoking God's Name, learned from אברהם's oath to his servant.

steps.title: רבינא asks whose view רב's statement follows
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי whether רב's statement, that the court uses the oath of אברהם, follows רבי חנינא בר אידי, who requires God's special name in an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: Whose opinion is this? Is it רבי חנינא בר אידי, who says we need God's special name?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא wants to know which opinion רב's statement in Step 24 follows. אברהם's oath used God's actual name, so maybe רב holds that an oath needs the special name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse רב quoted says 'בה׳', which is God's special four-letter name. That seems to fit רבי חנינא בר אידי, who requires that name. The question also hints at a problem: if so, רב would be going against the רבנן, who do not require it.

keyTerms.meaning: Like whom? Whose opinion does this follow?
God's special name, the four-letter name

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
Like whom? Like Rabbi Chanina bar Idi,
phrases.notes: He means רב's statement from the last step, about using אברהם's oath.

phrases.english: who says: we need the special name?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: כְּמַאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions which opinion רב's statement in Step 24 depends on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רב's 'oath of the Torah' mean the oath requires God's special name, following רבי חנינא בר אידי?

steps.title: רב אשי: the point is holding a holy object
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that רב can even follow the רבנן, who allow a substitute name for God. What רב learns from אברהם is that the person swearing must hold a holy object in his hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You can even say it follows the רבנן, who say a substitute name is enough. What we learn from it is that the person must hold an object in his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי says רב does not have to follow רבי חנינא בר אידי at all. רב's point is about holding a holy object, not about which name of God is used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אברהם had his servant put his hand under his thigh, holding something holy, while swearing. So 'the oath of the Torah' teaches that the person must physically hold a holy object. A substitute name for God can still be used, like the רבנן say.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say (the statement also fits this other opinion)
A substitute name for God, not the special name
The practical difference / what we learn from it
An object, here a holy object

steps.whyThisMatters: This changes what 'the oath of the Torah' means. It is about holding a holy object, not about saying God's special name.

phrases.english: He said to him: You can even say the Rabbis,
who say with a substitute name;
and what comes out from it is
he must hold an object in his hand.
phrases.notes: This comes from אברהם telling his servant to put his hand under his thigh while swearing (בראשית 24:2).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's question by explaining רב's statement differently.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב can follow the רבנן, who allow a substitute name. He is teaching that the person swearing must hold a holy object.

steps.title: רבא: an oath with God's name alone must be redone
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי's explanation fits רבא, who says a judge who gave an oath 'by ה׳, God of heaven' made a basic mistake, so the oath is redone.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this fits רבא, because רבא said: A judge who has someone swear 'by ה׳, God of heaven' is like someone who made a mistake in a clear משנה, and it is redone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from רבא for the idea that holding a holy object is required. Even saying God's name, as in אברהם's words, is not enough on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's judge used the exact words from the verse but did not have the person hold anything holy. רבא calls that a mistake in a clear משנה, which is a basic error. So the ruling is cancelled and the oath must be taken again. This shows that holding the holy object is the key part.

keyTerms.meaning: He had someone swear (he gave the oath)
Made a mistake in something clear and well-known, a basic error
Goes back; the ruling is cancelled and redone

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying God's name is wrong to use. The problem is that the judge used only the words and had the person hold no holy object.

phrases.english: And this is like Rava –
as Rava said:
This judge who had someone swear 'by the Lord, God of heaven' –
phrases.notes: These are אברהם's words from the verse in Step 24, said without holding anything holy.

phrases.english: is like one who made a mistake in a matter of the Mishna,
and it is redone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an Amora whose ruling matches רב אשי's explanation.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's claim that the oath requires holding a holy object
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's ruling that an oath with God's name alone, without a holy object, is a basic mistake and must be redone

steps.title: רב פפא: an oath on תפילין must be redone
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says a judge who had the person swear holding תפילין also made a basic mistake, so the oath is redone.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב פפא said: A judge who has someone swear holding תפילין is like someone who made a mistake in a clear משנה, and it is redone.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא adds a stricter rule. Holding a holy object is not enough; it must be the right object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא required some holy object in the hand. רב פפא goes further: תפילין are not good enough, and the person must hold a ספר תורה. If the judge used תפילין, the oath must be taken again.

keyTerms.meaning: Phylacteries, boxes holding verses from the Torah

phrases.english: And Rav Pappa said:
This judge who had someone swear with tefillin –
is like one who made a mistake in a matter of the Mishna,
and it is redone.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: הַאי דַּיָּינָא דְּאַשְׁבַּע בִּתְפִלִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second ruling about which object must be held, in the same pattern as רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath taken while holding תפילין instead of a ספר תורה must be redone.

steps.title: The הלכה follows רבא, not רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה follows רבא, because that person held no holy object. It does not follow רב פפא, because a person holding תפילין is still holding a holy object.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה follows רבא and not רב פפא. It follows רבא because the person did not hold an object in his hand. It does not follow רב פפא because the person did hold an object in his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling between רבא and רב פפא and explains the reason for each.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What matters is whether the person held a holy object at all. With God's name alone there was no object, so the oath is redone. With תפילין there was a holy object, so the oath stands even though it was not a ספר תורה.
steps.whatToRemember: A court oath requires holding a holy object, learned from אברהם's servant. Without any object the oath must be redone, but holding תפילין instead of a ספר תורה is still valid after the fact.

phrases.english: And the halacha is like Rava,
and the halacha is not like Rav Pappa.
The halacha is like Rava –
because he was not holding an object in his hand;
and the halacha is not like Rav Pappa –
because he was holding an object in his hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא כְּוָותֵיהּ דְּרָבָא, וְלֵית הִלְכְתָא כְּוָותֵיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between רבא (Step 27) and רב פפא (Step 28).
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An oath without any holy object in hand must be redone. An oath taken holding תפילין is valid after the fact.

steps.title: Standing or sitting, ספר תורה or תפילין
steps.stepSummary: A regular person swears standing and holding a ספר תורה. A תלמיד חכם swears sitting, and may hold תפילין from the outset.
steps.simpleTranslation: An oath is taken standing, but a תלמיד חכם may take it sitting. An oath is taken holding a ספר תורה, but a תלמיד חכם may hold תפילין even from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two practical rules for how the oath is carried out. Each rule has a different version for a תלמיד חכם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on steps 26–29, which taught that the person swearing must hold a holy object. The ordinary way is a ספר תורה. A תלמיד חכם may use תפילין even from the start, which fits step 29: תפילין also count as a holy object.

keyTerms.meaning: from the outset, as the normal first choice

steps.whatToRemember: The ordinary oath: standing, holding a ספר תורה. A תלמיד חכם: sitting, and תפילין are fine even from the start.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with רב פפא in step 28. The halacha did not follow him, so swearing with תפילין is not a mistake. Here it is allowed for a תלמיד חכם even from the start.

phrases.english: An oath is taken standing;
a Torah scholar takes it sitting.
An oath is taken with a Torah scroll;
a Torah scholar may use tefillin even from the outset.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the conclusion of step 29, that תפילין count as a holy object, into practical rules, and adds the standing/sitting rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ordinary person swears standing with a ספר תורה. A תלמיד חכם swears sitting and may use תפילין from the outset.

steps.title: The judges' oath may be said in any language
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the oath the judges give does not have to be said in Hebrew.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: the oath given by the judges may also be said in any language.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a new rule: the judges' oath may be said in any language the person understands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the topic was what the person holds and how he stands. Now the topic moves to the words of the oath. Hebrew is not required.

keyTerms.meaning: the oath imposed by the judges
in its own language, any language

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
The oath of the judges,
it too may be said in its own language.
phrases.notes: 'Its own language' means whatever language the person swearing speaks, not only Hebrew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how the oath is physically carried out to the language of the oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The judges' oath may be said in any language.

steps.title: The judges begin warning the person
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא starts to describe the warning the judges give before the oath: 'Be aware.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They say to him: Be aware,
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The ברייתא is starting to quote the warning the judges say before the oath, and the warning continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the person swears, the judges speak to him directly. 'Be aware' opens the warning, but the actual content has not come yet.

phrases.english: They say to him:
phrases.notes: 'They' are the judges, talking to the person about to swear.

phrases.english: Be aware,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and opens its description of the judges' warning before the oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before the oath, the judges warn the person, beginning with 'Be aware.'
